channel.title: The Fix by JB - Jonathan Barlow
channel.description: Insights on leadership, systems thinking, technology, and Detroit from Jonathan Barlow.

item.title: The Data Dashboard Nobody Checks
item.description: Cities spend millions building performance dashboards that no one uses to make decisions. Here's why the data isn't the problem — the system is.

item.title: The Soft Launch Is a Lie
item.description: Builders use 'soft launches' to delay accountability. Here's why that instinct kills momentum and what to do instead.

item.title: The Permit Is Not the Problem
item.description: Builders blame permits, but the real drag on housing is what surrounds them. A systems look at why approvals alone won't fix the shortage.

item.title: The Case for Boring Infrastructure
item.description: Flashy projects get the press. Reliable pipes, roads, and grids build cities. Here's why boring infrastructure is the actual work that matters.

item.title: Why the Gig Economy Is a Systems Failure Dressed as Flexibility
item.description: The gig economy isn't innovation — it's a broken labor system shifting risk onto workers. Here's what the data actually shows, and what we need to fix.

item.title: What Amazon HQ2 Taught Every City About Desperation
item.description: Amazon's HQ2 search exposed how cities compete against themselves. Here's what the bidding war actually revealed about economic development strategy.

item.title: The Invisible Tax on Being Small
item.description: Small businesses pay more per dollar to survive than large ones. It's not a market failure — it's a system design. Here's what that costs us.

item.title: Why Neighborhoods Need CFOs, Not Just Activists
item.description: Passion builds movements. Financial architecture builds neighborhoods. Here's why community development needs operators, not just advocates.

item.title: The Talent Pipeline Nobody Built
item.description: Detroit and cities like it keep importing skilled workers while ignoring the people already here. That's not a talent shortage. That's a system failure.

item.title: What Veterans Can Teach Us About Building Under Pressure
item.description: Veterans carry systems-thinking and pressure-tested leadership that most organizations desperately need. Here's what builders can learn from them.

item.title: Why Most Innovation Labs Don't Innovate
item.description: Innovation labs cost millions and produce little. Here's a systems diagnosis of why corporate and civic labs fail — and what actually moves the needle.

item.title: The Franchise Model for Social Impact: What Nonprofits Can Learn from McDonald's
item.description: The franchise model solves replication problems that kill most social impact work. Here's how mission-driven operators can borrow the playbook.

item.title: How to Build a Regional Economy That Actually Works
item.description: Regional economies fail when cities compete instead of coordinate. Here's the blueprint for building economic systems that actually strengthen entire regions.

item.title: Why Experience Should Be a Credential
item.description: Only 16% of skilled trade workers have college degrees, yet they build everything we depend on. We're measuring competence with the wrong tools.

item.title: The Real Cost of Free Programs
item.description: Why 'free' government and nonprofit programs create hidden costs that burden cities like Detroit. A systems analysis of dependency cycles and resource allocation.

item.title: What Happens When You Build Tech for Communities Instead of Consumers
item.description: Tech built for communities creates lasting infrastructure, not just user engagement. Analysis of Detroit, Austin, and Barcelona's community-first approaches.

item.title: Why Every City Needs an Operating System, Not Just a Strategic Plan
item.description: Cities waste billions on strategic plans that sit on shelves. Detroit and others are building real-time operating systems that actually execute change.

item.title: The Missing Layer Between Policy and People
item.description: Municipal policies fail because we've eliminated the human infrastructure that translates intent into action. Here's what cities must rebuild.

item.title: Why the Best Operators Never Apply for Grants
item.description: The most effective business operators avoid grants entirely. Here's why dependency on external funding kills operational discipline and long-term growth.

item.title: What Real Public-Private Partnerships Look Like
item.description: Most public-private partnerships fail because we misunderstand their purpose. Here's what successful P3s actually accomplish in Detroit, Denver, and beyond.

item.title: The Builder's Dilemma: Scale vs. Quality in Community Work
item.description: Community builders face an impossible choice: serve more people with less impact, or fewer people with deeper results. The data reveals which approach wins.

item.title: Why Most DEI Programs Produce Reports Instead of Results
item.description: A systems analysis of why diversity initiatives fail: measurement gaps, structural misalignment, and what cities like Detroit teach us about real change.

item.title: How Detroit's Comeback Story Gets Told Wrong Every Time
item.description: The media narrative misses Detroit's real recovery mechanics. Here's what actually drives urban renewal when you look at the systems, not the stories.

item.title: The Death of the Generalist and the Rise of the Systems Thinker
item.description: Traditional generalists are becoming obsolete. The future belongs to systems thinkers who can navigate complexity across interconnected domains.

item.title: Why Mentorship Programs Fail and Apprenticeship Models Work
item.description: Traditional mentorship programs show 70% dropout rates while apprenticeships deliver measurable outcomes. The difference lies in structure, not intent.

item.title: What Cannabis Legalization Taught Me About Regulatory Capture
item.description: Cannabis legalization exposed how regulatory capture works in practice. A systems analysis of what Detroit, Denver, and California teach us about policy design.

item.title: The Three Things Every City Gets Wrong About Economic Development
item.description: Most cities chase incentives and flashy projects while missing the fundamentals. A systems analysis of what actually drives urban economic growth.

item.title: Why Government Contracts Favor Companies That Don't Deliver
item.description: Government procurement systems reward proposal writers over builders. Here's why contracts go to companies that promise everything and deliver nothing.

item.title: The Operator Gap: Why Execution Talent Is the Scarcest Resource
item.description: Most businesses fail not from bad ideas, but from poor execution. The scarcest talent isn't visionaries—it's operators who can build and scale systems.

item.title: Stop Building Apps. Start Building Systems.
item.description: Why the app-first mentality is failing cities like Detroit. Real builders focus on interconnected systems that solve problems at scale.

item.title: What Happens When Community Development Meets Private Capital
item.description: Examining the tension between profit-driven investment and community needs through Detroit, Atlanta, and Portland's development patterns.

item.title: The Infrastructure Nobody Talks About: Digital Access in 2026
item.description: Detroit's digital divide reveals a critical infrastructure gap affecting 21% of households nationwide. Here's what builders need to know about connectivity as foundation.

item.title: Why Small Cities Are Outpacing Big Ones in Economic Recovery
item.description: Small cities like Boise and Grand Rapids show faster job growth and lower costs than major metros. Detroit's neighborhoods reveal the same pattern at micro scale.

item.title: The Workforce System Isn't Failing — It's Misaligned
item.description: Despite $3.6B in annual WIOA spending, employers can't fill roles. The workforce system works — just not for the outcomes we need.

item.title: We Fund Startups. We Don't Build Businesses
item.description: Detroit, Atlanta, and Philadelphia celebrate launches but ignore the operational infrastructure that keeps businesses alive past year three.

item.title: Why Cost of Living Relief Isn't Reaching Families
item.description: Inflation is cooling but families still struggle. The problem isn't lack of programs—it's delivery infrastructure that creates friction instead of flow.

item.title: America Isn't Broke — It's Disconnected
item.description: GDP hits records while 60% live paycheck to paycheck. The problem isn't money supply—it's that our systems can't connect dollars to outcomes.

item.title: Why Detroit Operators Outperform Silicon Valley Startups
item.description: Detroit businesses show higher survival rates than Valley startups. The difference isn't luck—it's fundamentally different operating principles.

item.title: The Real Measure of a City Isn't GDP — It's Whether People Stay
item.description: Detroit's population decline masks a deeper truth about urban success. We measure the wrong metrics while the real indicator sits in plain sight.

item.title: Trust Is Shifting From Institutions to Operators
item.description: Government trust at 22%. But trust isn't disappearing — it's relocating to operators who deliver results.

item.title: The Real Gap in America Is Execution
item.description: Every city has a strategic plan. Most say the same things. The plans are fine. The execution systems don't exist.

item.title: Why Billions in Funding Aren't Producing Results
item.description: Follow the money. $2.6 trillion flows through nonprofits. 70% of programs disappear when funding ends. The money is there. The coordination isn't.

item.title: Programs Don't Scale — Systems Do
item.description: Programs have start dates and end dates. Systems have feedback loops. The question isn't "did the program work?" — it's "did the system change?"

item.title: Opportunity Isn't Missing — It's Not Organized
item.description: In every city there are grants, programs, accelerators, training, capital. The resources exist. What doesn't exist is a map.

item.title: We Don't Have a Youth Problem — We Have a Pathway Problem
item.description: 4.5 million young people not in school or working. The conversation focuses on behavior. But behavior follows design.

item.title: Why Families Are Carrying the Weight of Broken Systems
item.description: When every other system fails, families are the last safety net. That's not resilience — it's structural failure being absorbed by the people least equipped to carry it.

item.title: Childcare Is the Hidden Economic Infrastructure
item.description: Average childcare costs $10,853/year per child. 57% of parents have turned down work because of it. Childcare isn't a social issue — it's economic infrastructure.

item.title: The Housing Crisis Is a Coordination Crisis
item.description: Detroit has 70,000 vacant lots. The national narrative says we need more housing. The real issue isn't supply — it's coordination.

item.title: AI Is Exposing a Bigger Problem Than Job Loss
item.description: 300 million jobs globally could be affected. But AI isn't replacing strong systems — it's exposing fragile ones we've been hiding behind.

item.title: Training Programs Don't Create Careers — Systems Do
item.description: Only 37% of workforce trainees are employed in their trained field at one year. A training program is one node. A career requires six.

item.title: The Workforce System Isn't Failing — It's Misaligned
item.description: $3.6 billion spent on workforce development annually. 87% of employers still can't find talent. The system isn't failing — it was never aligned.

item.title: We Fund Startups. We Don't Build Businesses.
item.description: 5.5 million new business applications filed last year. Half will close within five years. We celebrate the launch but nobody builds the boring middle.

item.title: America Isn't Broke — It's Disconnected
item.description: GDP is up. Markets are up. Employment is technically strong. But 60% of Americans still live paycheck to paycheck. The problem isn't money — it's architecture.

item.title: Why Your Network Isn't Working
item.description: You collect connections but don't build systems around them. Your network fails because you treat it like a Rolodex instead of infrastructure.

item.title: Build for the Person Who Stays
item.description: Most urban projects build for the "ideal user" who doesn't exist. Real impact means building for the person who stayed through every crisis.

item.title: Why Every Crisis is an Innovation Opportunity
item.description: Three years ago, Detroit's water infrastructure failed. While others saw catastrophe, I saw a laboratory for building resilient urban systems.

item.title: Programs vs. Systems: Why Detroit Keeps Starting Over
item.description: Detroit doesn't have a program problem. It has a systems problem. Every year, new initiatives launch with press releases and ribbon cuttings, yet the same problems persist.

item.title: Most Leadership Advice Is Backwards
item.description: They tell you to think big and start small. I say think in systems and start with structure.
